label: Two-Way Tables
overview: A two-way table (also called a contingency table) organises data about two categorical variables. Each cell shows the count (or frequency) for a specific combination. SAT questions ask you to read values, compute row/column/grand totals, calculate probabilities (basic and conditional), and identify associations between variables.

keyFormulas.name: Conditional probability from table
keyFormulas.latex: P(A \mid B) = \dfrac{\text{count in A and B}}{\text{row or column total for B}}

keyFormulas.name: Joint probability
keyFormulas.latex: P(A \text{ and } B) = \dfrac{\text{cell count for A \cap B}}{\text{grand total}}

workedExamples.problem: In a class of 40 students, 25 play sport. Of those 25, 10 also play an instrument. Of the 15 non-sport students, 8 play an instrument. What is the probability that a randomly chosen student plays an instrument given they play sport?

steps.title: Identify the conditional setup
steps.content: We want P(instrument | sport). The condition restricts us to the 25 sport students.

steps.title: Apply conditional probability
steps.content: 10 of the 25 sport students play an instrument.

commonMistakes.mistake: Using the grand total as denominator for a conditional probability question
commonMistakes.fix: Conditional probability restricts the sample space. Use the row or column total of the given condition, not the grand total.

commonMistakes.mistake: Misreading which category is the condition vs. the event
commonMistakes.fix: P(A | B) means: among the B group, find the fraction that is also A. B is the condition (denominator), A is the event (numerator from the intersection cell).

quickTip: Build the table yourself if it's described in words — filling in the totals first often makes the numbers obvious. Label rows and columns clearly before computing any probability.
